title: Spatial Navigation and Negative Emotions: The Effect of Emotion Processing on Wayfinding and Visuospatial Working Memory
central_proposition: Processing others' negative emotional expressions, particularly fearful faces, influences spatial navigation abilities and visuospatial working memory performance, with significant modulation by gender differences and the specific type of emotional stimulus.

concept_definitions.name: Spatial Navigation
concept_definitions.definition: The ability to locate oneself in space and traverse physical environments.

concept_definitions.name: Wayfinding
concept_definitions.definition: Successfully identifying a destination and creating a route to reach it, embodying the strategic and purposeful component of navigation.

concept_definitions.name: Emotions
concept_definitions.definition: Subjective experiences characterised by feelings, thoughts, and physiological responses that play a central role in shaping behaviour, decision-making and social interactions.

concept_definitions.name: Cognitive Map
concept_definitions.definition: Internal mental images of physical spaces that animals and humans use to navigate the real world, especially to discover new shortcuts.

concept_definitions.name: Locomotion
concept_definitions.definition: The real-time aspect of navigation, requiring the skilled execution of movement in the desired direction while avoiding collisions or obstacles.

concept_definitions.name: Orientation
concept_definitions.definition: Maintaining a sense of place while moving, relying on landmark-based updating and dead reckoning or path integration.

concept_definitions.name: Landmark-based updating
concept_definitions.definition: Recognition of specific features or locations in the environment, drawing on either internal or external memory.

concept_definitions.name: Path integration
concept_definitions.definition: Continuously updating one's position and orientation based on self-motion cues, helping to maintain a sense of place in unfamiliar environments.

concept_definitions.name: Visuospatial Working Memory (VSWM)
concept_definitions.definition: A specific type of working memory that plays a crucial role in retrieving and manipulating mental images, maintaining spatial orientation, and tracking moving objects.

concept_definitions.name: Theory of Mind (ToM)
concept_definitions.definition: A mechanism that underlies a crucial aspect of social competence, namely the ability to infer mental states: that is, to know that other people know, want, feel, or believe things.

concept_definitions.name: Mirror Neurons
concept_definitions.definition: Neurons, located predominantly in motor areas, known to fire when observing the actions of others, providing individuals with an understanding of the intentions behind these actions.

concept_definitions.name: Valence
concept_definitions.definition: The inherent positivity or negativity of an emotion.

concept_definitions.name: Arousal
concept_definitions.definition: The intensity or activation level of an emotion, ranging from mild and barely perceptible to intense and overwhelming.

concept_definitions.name: Spatial anxiety
concept_definitions.definition: Negative emotions specific to spatial contexts.

argument_structure: The dissertation first reviews the existing literature on spatial navigation and emotion processing, highlighting the limited understanding of their interplay. It then identifies specific gaps related to stimulus type (faces, bodies, contexts), emotion type (fear, anger), gender differences, and the involvement of visuospatial working memory. A series of experiments are proposed to empirically test these relationships, and the findings are synthesized to build a more comprehensive conceptual framework.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The proposed causal mechanisms involve: 1) **Attention Capture and Resource Allocation**: Threatening emotional stimuli, particularly fearful faces, are evolutionarily salient and capture attention, diverting cognitive resources (especially VSWM) from ongoing spatial tasks. 2) **Threat Specificity**: Fear signals ambiguous, general threats, leading to sustained vigilance and broader attention, potentially causing prolonged interference. Anger signals immediate, directed threats, which may dissipate once the source is gone, leading to less sustained interference. 3) **Gender Differences in Cognitive Load Management and Emotion Regulation**: Males and females differ in how they process emotions and manage cognitive resources. Females may be better at emotion recognition and regulation, allowing them to better control the influence of emotional stimuli on cognitive tasks, while males may experience greater VSWM resource depletion. 4) **Face-Specificity**: Faces, as social stimuli, possess high communicative value and efficiently signal potential danger, making them more influential than body expressions or contextual scenes in modulating navigation. 5) **Neural Overlaps**: Spatial cognition and emotion processing rely on shared neural networks (e.g., hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, amygdala), leading to potential interference or modulation when both are engaged.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Processing emotional facial expressions will influence participants' behavioural tendencies and wayfinding performance (Q1).
The effect of emotional stimuli on navigation will be face-specific, differing from body expressions or contextual scenes (Q2).
Fearful and angry facial expressions will affect spatial navigation differently, with fear potentially causing more sustained interference (Q2).
Gender differences will modulate spatial navigation performance and the effect of negative facial emotions on it (Q3).
Fearful or angry facial expressions will influence specific spatial navigation domains (landmark, location, path knowledge) differently (Q4).
The influence of negative emotional processing on navigation will be mediated by competition for visuospatial working memory resources (Q5).
bridge_warrants: The interplay between emotion processing and spatial navigation is rooted in evolutionary psychology, where threat detection is crucial for survival (Ekman, 1993).
Cognitive load theory explains how emotional stimuli can deplete shared visuospatial working memory resources, impacting performance on concurrent or subsequent tasks (Curby et al., 2019).

Social cognition theories, such as emotional contagion and Theory of Mind, provide mechanisms for how observing others' emotions can influence an individual's affective state and behavior (Hatfield et al., 1993).

Neuroscience research on neural overlaps between spatial navigation (hippocampus, prefrontal cortex) and emotion processing (amygdala) suggests a biological basis for their interaction and potential interference (LeDoux, 2000).
methodological_critiques: Previous research on emotion processing and spatial navigation has largely overlooked the impact of processing *others'* emotions on navigation.
Existing studies often do not compare the effects of different emotional stimuli (faces, bodies, contexts) within the same framework.
Many studies on VSWM and emotion do not consider gender differences, which are crucial for both domains.
The role of task relevance (emotional stimuli being relevant vs. irrelevant to the primary task) in modulating emotional influence on cognition is often not explicitly tested.
model_structure: The paper implicitly proposes a conceptual model where external emotional stimuli (faces, bodies, scenes) are processed, leading to differential cognitive load and attentional allocation, which in turn modulates performance on spatial navigation tasks (wayfinding, landmark, location, path knowledge) and visuospatial working memory. This entire process is moderated by individual differences, particularly gender, due to varying cognitive resource management and emotion regulation strategies. The model emphasizes a face-specific and emotion-specific (fear vs. anger) effect, with underlying neural overlaps between spatial and emotional processing.
limitations: The virtual reality environments used were small-scale (office building), which may limit generalizability to larger outdoor environments.
Some experiments had small and unbalanced sample sizes, potentially limiting statistical power and inference.
The studies primarily used static 2D images of stimuli, which may limit the sense of presence and ecological validity compared to dynamic, multimodal stimuli.
The research focused on task-irrelevant emotional stimuli, and the effects might differ if stimuli were task-relevant.
The studies primarily investigated negative emotions, with limited exploration of positive emotions.
Behavioral measures of attention (e.g., eye tracking) were not included, which could provide further insights into attentional patterns.
Age ranges varied across experiments, potentially introducing inconsistencies in results related to natural declines in navigation functionality.

paper_metadata.title: Recombinant Enaction: Manipulatives Generate New Procedures in the Imagination, by Extending and Recombining Action Spaces
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Recombinant Enaction: Manipulatives Generate New Procedures in the Imagination, by Extending and Recombining Action Spaces
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractManipulation of physical models such as tangrams and tiles is a popular approach to teaching early mathematics concepts. This pedagogical approach is extended by new computational media, where mathematical entities such as equations and vectors can be virtually manipulated. The cognitive and neural mechanisms supporting such manipulation‐based learning—particularly how actions generate new internal structures that support problem‐solving—are not understood. We develop a model of the way manipulations generate internal traces embedding actions, and how these action‐traces recombine during problem‐solving. This model is based on a study of two groups of sixth‐grade students solving area problems. Before problem‐solving, one group manipulated a tangram, the other group answered a descriptive test. Eye‐movement trajectories during problem‐solving were different between the groups. A second study showed that this difference required the tangram's geometrical structure, just manipulation was not enough. We propose a theoretical model accounting for these results, and discuss its implications.
